note: Screen 12. Planet positions come from data/ephemeris_mer.json (JPL Horizons). Slider ranges, fuel, tolerance and stars are SIMULATED GAME VALUES.

physics.note: dvPerPower: AU/day of extra speed per power step (about 0.49 km/s); hitAU: how close counts as reaching Mars (game tolerance). The green WINDOW zone is computed live: launch days where a medium burn at about 0 degrees reaches Mars.

rules.title: 1. WAIT FOR THE WINDOW
rules.text: Earth and Mars line up for the most energy-efficient trip only about once every 26 months. Launch when Mars is the right amount ahead of Earth: in mid-2003 it was about 20 to 30 degrees ahead (real JPL Horizons positions).

rules.title: 2. BURN WITH EARTH'S MOTION
rules.text: Fire the engine in the direction Earth is already moving. The Sun's pull does the rest.

rules.title: 3. COAST HALF AN ORBIT
rules.text: Your path is a transfer orbit that touches both orbits. For Spirit and Opportunity the trip took about 7 months.

briefingMentor: Less fuel = more budget for science. Faster paths cost much more fuel!

tutorial.title: MENTOR STEP 1: LAUNCH DAY
tutorial.text: Drag the launch day and watch Mars move along its orbit (real JPL Horizons positions). Launch inside the green zone: Mars is about 20 to 30 degrees ahead of Earth, so you both meet at the same place.

tutorial.title: MENTOR STEP 2: BURN POWER
tutorial.text: Power sets how far your path reaches. Too weak and the path turns back before Mars. More power arrives sooner, but past the sweet spot it just burns fuel.

tutorial.title: MENTOR STEP 3: BURN DIRECTION
tutorial.text: Aiming away from Earth's motion wastes speed and bends your path. At 0° (prograde) you add to the speed Earth already gives you.

tutorial.title: MENTOR STEP 4: ENGAGE
tutorial.text: Press ENGAGE (or SPACE) to fly your plan. Remember: this is a TRANSFER trajectory from Earth to Mars, not an orbit around Mars.

day.title: [?] LAUNCH DAY
lines: Earth and Mars move at different speeds.
• Good windows come only about every 26 months.
• In the green zone (mid-2003) Mars is about 20 to 30 degrees ahead of Earth.

power.title: [?] BURN POWER
lines: How hard the engine pushes at launch.
• Too weak: the path never reaches Mars's orbit.
• Sweet spot: just enough to reach Mars, saves fuel.
• Too strong: arrives sooner, but wastes fuel you need later.

dir.title: [?] BURN DIRECTION
lines: • Toward or away from the Sun bends and shortens your path.

feedback.weak: Too weak! Your path turns back before reaching Mars's orbit. Try a bit more power, not the maximum.
feedback.late: You reach Mars's orbit, but Mars is not there yet (or already gone). Change the LAUNCH DAY so Mars is about 44° ahead.
feedback.dir: Your burn is pointing away from Earth's motion. Try a direction closer to 0°.
feedback.hog: You hit Mars, but you burned a lot of fuel! More power is not always better.
feedback.good: Great orbit! In the window, near 0° and medium power: the same idea NASA used for Spirit and Opportunity.
feedback.drawGood: Your drawn guess curved the same way as the real path: around the Sun, with Earth's motion. Nice intuition!
feedback.drawBad: Compare your drawing with the real path: spacecraft don't fly straight to Mars. They curve around the Sun in a transfer orbit.
feedback.transfer: This is a TRANSFER trajectory: half an ellipse around the Sun that starts at Earth's orbit and ends at Mars's orbit. It is not an orbit around Mars.
feedback.balance: The balance: launch window (when), fuel (how much power) and travel time (how fast). More power is not always better.

real.text: Real mission: Spirit launched June 10, 2003 and Opportunity July 7, 2003 (July 8 UTC); after about 7 months of cruise they arrived in January 2004.

angleNote: The textbook rule (44 degrees ahead) assumes circular orbits. With the real 2003 positions the efficient launch was with Mars about 20 to 30 degrees ahead.
